title: China’s EV Market Is Booming. There’s Just One Problem
gist: China's EV fleet is entering its first mass battery-retirement wave — 400,000 metric tons of battery waste last year, projected at 22.39 million tons by 2040 — and although certified recycling capacity exceeds retirement volume, certified firms process only about a quarter of it because informal operators that skip testing and pollution control can outbid them. Meanwhile the three largest North American recyclers (Ascend Elements, Li-Cycle, Lithion) have all gone through insolvency, underlining that battery recycling remains structurally unprofitable outside China's scale.

insights.claim: Annual sales of battery-powered vehicles in China rose from about 1 million in 2018 to more than 16 million in 2025, and with EV batteries typically lasting about eight years the country is entering its first major wave of battery retirements.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: The eight-year lag means the 2018–2020 sales cohort sets recycling volumes now, and the 16-million-unit cohort sets them from 2033 — a forecastable feedstock curve for recyclers.
insights.quote: Annual sales of battery-powered vehicles in China, including fully electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids, have surged from about 1 million in 2018 to more than 16 million in 2025.
insights.locator: After spending the past decade building the world’s largest electric vehicle market

insights.claim: China reported 400,000 metric tons of EV battery waste last year, and a joint China–US study projects 1.69 million metric tons in 2030 and 22.39 million metric tons by 2040 — a roughly 56-fold increase in 15 years.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Feedstock volume, not technology, will be the sector's defining variable; capacity buildouts sized to today's tonnage will be obsolete within a decade.
insights.quote: China reported 400,000 metric tons of EV battery waste last year. A joint study by researchers in China and the United States projected that the figure could grow to 1.69 million metric tons in 2030 and 22.39 million metric tons by 2040.
insights.locator: The number of batteries requiring disposal or reprocessing

insights.claim: Governments knowingly accelerated EV adoption before end-of-life infrastructure existed, betting that recycling systems would catch up — a deferred liability now coming due.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: The same 'infrastructure will catch up' bet is embedded in current policy on grid storage and solar panel waste; the EV battery case is the first test of whether it pays off.
insights.quote: Governments largely chose to accelerate EV adoption anyway, betting that recycling systems would eventually catch up.
insights.locator: For years, critics of electric vehicles have argued

themes.theme: Certified capacity exists — utilization does not

insights.claim: By 2023 China's certified recyclers had 623,000 metric tons of annual processing capacity, more than 1.5 times the volume of batteries retired that year, yet they handled only about 25 percent of those batteries.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: The bottleneck is feedstock capture, not plant capacity — so policy that redirects supply, not subsidies for new plants, is what moves recycler utilization and margins.
insights.quote: By 2023, certified companies had a combined annual processing capacity of 623,000 metric tons, more than 1.5 times the volume of batteries retired that year. Yet they handled only about 25 percent of those batteries
insights.locator: China began developing a formal EV battery recycling system as early as 2018

insights.claim: An investigation by Chinese financial outlet Yicai found that more than 100 of the 150-plus companies on the government's recycling 'white list' were no longer operating or could not be reached, meaning official capacity figures overstate real capability.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Treat Chinese certified-capacity statistics as a ceiling with a large phantom component — a direct warning against sizing the market off white-list registrations.
insights.quote: Its reporters attempted to contact every company on the white list and found that more than 100 were no longer operating or could not be reached.
insights.locator: An investigation published earlier this year by Yicai

insights.claim: Informal recyclers can outbid certified ones for used batteries precisely because they avoid the costs of safe testing, dismantling and pollution control — an adverse-selection loop that structurally starves compliant operators of feedstock.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: No amount of certified capacity fixes this without enforcement or a price floor; the compliant business model is only viable if the informal channel is closed.
insights.quote: They can pay more for used batteries because they avoid many of the costs associated with safe testing, dismantling, and pollution control.
insights.locator: A sprawling network of informal operators

insights.claim: Uncertified recyclers processed nearly 270,000 metric tons of retired batteries in 2023, and without decisive intervention the informal channel is projected to carry 1.26 million tons by 2030 and 16.79 million tons by 2040.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: On the base case, roughly three quarters of retired battery tonnage stays in the grey market through 2040 — the single biggest downside scenario for recovered-material supply.
insights.quote: Sun’s research estimated that uncertified recyclers handled nearly 270,000 metric tons of retired batteries in 2023.
insights.locator: Unlicensed recyclers, lacking in technology and infrastructure

insights.claim: Academic researchers characterize China's attempt to control the informal battery-recycling market as a 'losing battle', indicating specialists do not expect current enforcement to work.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Expert pessimism on enforcement argues against assuming policy-driven step-changes in certified recycler volumes.
insights.quote: researchers described China’s effort to control the informal market as a “losing battle.”
insights.locator: In the paper, “The Urgency to Regulate Informal EV Battery Recycling in China,”

themes.theme: Physical and safety externalities of grey-market processing

insights.claim: A 2024 case in Jiangxi Province saw an uncertified company improperly dismantle 364 metric tons of waste lithium iron phosphate batteries, killing vegetation across 6 acres of forest and more than 420 cubic feet of standing timber.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Documented site-scale damage from a single 364-ton batch gives a concrete damage-per-ton anchor for pricing the environmental liability of informal processing.
insights.quote: The resulting contamination caused vegetation to die across 6 acres of forest and killed more than 420 cubic feet of standing timber.
insights.locator: In a case announced in Jiangxi Province in 2024

insights.claim: Untested cells salvaged by unlicensed operators are being resold into unapproved applications such as aftermarket range-extending battery packs, creating substantial fire risk — a Xiaomi SU7 sedan fire in Changzhou was attributed by its owner to an aftermarket range extender rather than the factory battery.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Aftermarket cell reuse creates fire incidents that get attributed to the OEM brand — a reputational and warranty-cost channel automakers cannot control directly.
insights.quote: The owner later told the Sanxiang Metropolis Daily that the battery involved was an aftermarket range extender rather than the vehicle’s original factory-installed battery.
insights.locator: In November, a Xiaomi SU7 electric sedan caught fire

insights.claim: Repurposing retired packs for second-life use is technically complex and expensive because recyclers must test and grade batteries, modules and sometimes individual cells — a Tesla Model Y pack alone can contain more than 4,000 cells.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Cell-level grading cost is why second-life storage businesses keep failing to scale; automated diagnostics is the enabling technology to watch.
insights.quote: A Tesla Model Y battery pack, for example, can contain more than 4,000 individual cells.
insights.locator: Repurposing, however, requires recyclers to test and grade batteries

insights.claim: Material recovery is the more commercially promising route: batteries are processed into 'black mass' containing lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese and graphite, with advanced processes recovering more than 95 percent of certain critical battery materials.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: >95 percent recovery makes recycled feedstock a genuine substitute for mined critical minerals at scale — a long-term structural headwind for primary lithium and nickel demand growth.
insights.quote: Some advanced processes can recover more than 95 percent of certain critical battery materials.
insights.locator: Recycling batteries into raw materials appears to offer a more commercially promising path

insights.claim: Unlicensed recyclers cannot reach high recovery rates because they lack the technology and infrastructure, so grey-market processing permanently destroys critical-mineral value rather than merely relocating it.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Every ton diverted to informal channels is a ton of lithium, cobalt and nickel that never returns to supply — a bullish tail risk for primary miners if enforcement stays weak.
insights.quote: Unlicensed recyclers, lacking in technology and infrastructure, are unlikely to achieve such high recovery rates.
insights.locator: Unlicensed recyclers, lacking in technology and infrastructure

themes.theme: Policy: extended producer responsibility and the battery passport

insights.claim: A new national EV battery recycling regulation took effect on April 1, modeled on Europe's 'battery passport' approach, requiring automakers to bear greater responsibility for collection and mandating that retired-vehicle batteries be routed through approved channels to certified processors.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Extended producer responsibility moves the collection cost onto OEM balance sheets — a new per-vehicle cost line for Chinese automakers and a guaranteed volume channel for certified recyclers.
insights.quote: China is adopting a similar approach to Europe’s “battery passport” system, requiring automakers to bear greater responsibility for collecting and recycling used batteries.
insights.locator: A new national regulation governing EV battery recycling took effect on April 1

insights.claim: Modeled policy intervention — automaker responsibility, stricter controls on informal recyclers, and incentives for consumers and certified firms — could raise certified handling to 60 percent of retired EV batteries by 2030 and 92 percent by 2060.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: A jump from 25 percent to 60 percent capture by 2030 would more than double certified-recycler throughput — the key upside scenario for the compliant recycling sector.
insights.quote: certified companies could handle 60 percent of retired EV batteries by 2030 and 92 percent by 2060, the study concluded.
insights.locator: Under such a scenario

insights.claim: Researchers argue the fix requires automakers to absorb higher costs and consumers to accept lower resale prices rather than selling to informal recyclers, meaning the solution is priced rather than technological.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Compliance costs land on OEM margins and consumer residual values — both under-modeled in current EV total-cost-of-ownership assumptions.
insights.quote: Automakers have to take responsibility, even if it pushes up costs,
insights.locator: But more needs to be done, said Sun

themes.theme: Western recyclers are failing while China consolidates the lead

insights.claim: Ascend Elements raised more than $1 billion after 2021 and built facilities in Georgia and Kentucky, but high construction costs, weaker US EV demand and uncertainty over federal support pushed it into Chapter 11 bankruptcy in April.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: A billion dollars of private capital was insufficient against soft feedstock demand and policy uncertainty — a direct read-through for anyone underwriting US battery-materials buildouts.
insights.quote: But high construction costs, weaker EV demand in the US, and uncertainty surrounding federal support made its expansion difficult to sustain. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in April.
insights.locator: Ascend Elements invested heavily in facilities in Georgia and Kentucky

insights.claim: The two other major North American battery recyclers, Li-Cycle and Lithion Technologies, both entered insolvency proceedings in 2025, with Glencore taking over Li-Cycle — leaving commodity traders rather than specialists holding Western recycling assets.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Distressed consolidation into Glencore means Western recycling capacity ends up inside a diversified commodity balance sheet that can absorb negative carry — the only viable owner structure at current economics.
insights.quote: Two other major North American battery recyclers, Li-Cycle and Lithion Technologies, entered insolvency proceedings in 2025.
insights.locator: “We are the first of its kind,” Yan Wang said

insights.claim: Battery recycling has proven difficult to make profitable worldwide, so China's dominance stems from feedstock volume rather than superior economics — it has become the global leader in EV battery recycling because it has the batteries.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Scale of retired-battery supply is the moat; Western recyclers cannot close the gap until their own fleets age, implying a decade of Chinese control over recycled critical-mineral flows.
insights.quote: With a vast and rapidly growing supply of used batteries, China has also emerged as the global leader in EV battery recycling.
insights.locator: Yan Wang and Sun agreed that China has sufficient certified recycling capacity

insights.claim: How Beijing handles battery retirement will set the template other countries copy, because China leads global EV adoption and will hit every end-of-life problem first.
insights.speaker: Andrew Liu
insights.so_what: Chinese recycling regulation is a leading indicator for what US and EU rules will look like — watch it for the shape of future compliance costs elsewhere.
insights.quote: Because China leads the world in EV adoption, how Beijing manages both the risks and opportunities of battery retirement could help shape the industry’s global model.
